summary: This informational RFC defines the canonical link relation, which designates an IRI as preferred over resources with duplicate content.

eli5.summary: If the same page lives at many addresses, a tag points to the main one, so search engines know which to use.

subtitle: A link tag to mark a page's preferred version when duplicates exist

tldr.problem: Search engines and other crawlers index duplicate content separately, wasting resources and diluting ranking signals when the same content appears at multiple URLs (e.g., with tracking parameters or split across multiple pages).
tldr.mechanism: The canonical link relation is an HTML tag or HTTP header that authors place on duplicate pages to designate a single preferred version, telling search engines to consolidate indexing and ranking to that URL.
tldr.outcome: Search engines and crawlers can focus processing on the canonical version, consolidate link popularity to a single URL, and reduce wasted effort indexing duplicates.

facts.label: Placement options
facts.value: HTML link tag or HTTP Link header

facts.label: Target domain
facts.value: Can be same or different domain

today: RFC 6596 is an Informational document published in April 2012. It has not been obsoleted. The canonical link relation is widely implemented by Google, Bing, and Yahoo, and is a standard practice for managing duplicate content across the web.

sections.title: The Canonical Link Relation
sections.content:
Web pages often appear at multiple URLs: a product page might be accessed at /product?id=42, /product?id=42&category=electronics, or /product?id=42&session=xyz789. The content is identical or nearly so, but each URL is crawled and indexed separately, diluting ranking signals and wasting resources.

The canonical link relation lets an author designate a preferred URL. This is done by adding a link tag in the HTML head or as an HTTP header. Applications such as search engines can then treat the other URLs as duplicates of the canonical, consolidate indexing and link popularity, and focus crawling effort on the preferred version.
sections.eli5: When your page lives at multiple addresses, you can point to the main one. Search engines then treat the others as copies and don't index them separately.

sections.title: Syntax and Usage
sections.content:
The canonical link can be placed in HTML as a <link> tag with rel="canonical", pointing to the canonical URL via an href attribute. For example, a product page can declare a link to the clean version without session parameters. Relative URLs are also allowed.

Alternatively, it can be sent as an HTTP header with the Link header field. An author SHOULD specify only one canonical link per page; multiple canonicals create confusion.

The target URL may be on a different domain, use a different scheme (http to https), be self-referential (pointing to itself), or be a superset of the content (e.g., a multi-page article pointing to a single-page view). However, the content at the canonical URL MUST be either the same as or a superset of the content on the page declaring it.
sections.eli5: You add a tag in the page that says where the main copy is. Or you send it in a message to the browser. Only one canonical per page.

sections.title: Implementation Guidelines
sections.content:
Several guidelines help ensure canonicals work correctly. The target URL SHOULD NOT be the destination of a permanent HTTP redirect (301 or 300 status codes), because redirects already signal that content has moved. The target should not itself declare a canonical to another URL (no chaining). It should not return an error code like 404. And in multi-page articles, page-2.html should not declare page-1.html canonical, because that would lose the content from page 2.

When the canonical points to a superset (e.g., individual pages declaring a 'view all' version as canonical), be mindful of user experience. The user following a link to page 2 suddenly being served the full article might be disorienting or load slowly.

Before adding a canonical, verify that the target content truly duplicates or contains the source content, and that permanent redirects could not serve the same purpose.
sections.eli5: Don't point to a permanently moved page, or to a page that points elsewhere. Don't break multi-page articles by claiming the first page is canonical. Check that the canonical actually has the right content.

sections.title: Error Handling and Security
sections.content:
If a canonical is declared improperly—such as chained canonicals, pointing to an error page, or creating confusion—applications are expected to use their own heuristics to recover. Some may ignore the malformed canonical and continue processing normally.

Canonicals are vulnerable to abuse: if a site is compromised, an attacker can declare a malicious site as the canonical, causing search engines to treat the legitimate content as a duplicate and transfer ranking signals to the attacker's site. A non-compromised site can also provide misleading canonicals, whether intentionally or through misconfiguration.

IANA registered the canonical relation as per RFC 5988 to ensure a single, standardized meaning across applications.
sections.eli5: If you mess up the canonical, applications ignore it and move on. Hackers can abuse it to steal ranking by declaring their site canonical. That's why being careful matters.
